questions.q: Show that the Arms Act of 1878 cannot be described as a law that disarmed everyone in British India equally.
questions.a: The Act prohibited Indians from keeping arms, but it allowed the British to do so. A law that takes weapons from one group and leaves them with another is not an equal disarmament. It fits the chapter's picture of Indians being treated as inferior to the British.
s: States what the Act prohibited for Indians
States that it allowed the British to keep arms
Concludes that this is unequal treatment, fitting the chapter's account of inferior status

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Missionary activity in India went on after 1858 even though the proclamation promised there would be no attempt to impose Christianity.
Reason (R): The proclamation was issued in Queen Victoria's name.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: A pamphlet of the time says: 'Indians are treated as belonging to an inferior race.' Write three short situations, one on pay, one on courts and one on public places, that could be cited in it.
questions.a: Pay: an Indian lecturer in a university is paid less than a British lecturer in the same post. Courts: a European accused of harming an Indian is tried before a jury with a British majority which is lenient to him. Public places: an Indian is not allowed to enter a club or sit in a railway compartment where Europeans mix.
s: A situation on unequal pay for the same post
A situation on a British-majority jury being lenient
A situation on exclusion from clubs, trains or other public spaces

questions.q: In a famine-hit district in the 1880s, a student writes the chain of hardship in the order the chapter gives it. Which sequence is correct?
questions.a: Heavy land taxes, then several severe famines, then widespread discontent among peasants and tribals
o: Heavy land taxes, then several severe famines, then widespread discontent among peasants and tribals
Several severe famines, then heavy land taxes, then widespread discontent
Cheap British goods, then heavy land taxes, then several severe famines
Widespread discontent, then heavy land taxes, then several severe famines

questions.q: A European is tried in an Indian court for a crime against an Indian. According to the chapter, why might the result be lenient?
questions.a: Most juries had a British majority, lenient towards crimes by Europeans against 'natives'
o: Most juries had a British majority, lenient towards crimes by Europeans against 'natives'
The Arms Act directed the courts to excuse any European found carrying a weapon
The Vernacular Press Act barred newspapers from reporting any trial involving a European defendant
The proclamation of 1858 placed every European above the law of the land in India

questions.q: Rohan says: 'The 1858 proclamation changed nothing; the Company was simply replaced by a new name.' Test his claim against the chapter and give your verdict.
questions.a: Partly right. He is right that the assurances were not respected in practice and the economic exploitation continued: heavy land taxes, famines and cheap British goods. But 'nothing' is too strong, because the Crown did take direct control from the Company, with the Secretary of State and the Viceroy governing in the Queen's name, and the promises were meant to convey that the rulers would prefer to rule in peace rather than by military force.
s: Accepts what is right: assurances not respected, exploitation continued
Rejects 'nothing': direct Crown control through the Secretary of State and Viceroy, and a changed message
Verdict: partly right

questions.q:
Two students summarise Crown rule after 1858. Anil says: 'The promises of 1858 were fine words, but the hardships continued.' Bela says: 'After 1858 Indians were treated as equals, as promised.'
(a) What did the proclamation promise the 'natives' of the Indian territories?
(b) Give one example from the chapter of Indians being treated as inferior to the British.
(c) Give one economic hardship from the chapter that continued after 1858.
(d) Decide which student's summary the chapter supports, and say which of your answers (b) and (c) settles it.
questions.a: (a) That they would be taken care of just like all other subjects and that there would be no attempt to impose Christianity on any of them. (b) Any one of: lesser pay for Indians in the same posts in the army, civil services or universities; British-majority juries lenient towards Europeans; exclusion from clubs, trains and public spaces; the Arms Act; the Vernacular Press Act. (c) Any one of: heavy land taxes leading to severe famines; cheap British-manufactured goods that local industries could not compete with. (d) Anil's: the chapter says none of the assurances were respected in practice, and answers (b) and (c) show unequal treatment and continuing hardship, which contradict Bela's claim of equal treatment.
s: Part (a): care like all other subjects; no imposition of Christianity
Part (b): one example of unequal treatment
Part (c): one continuing economic hardship
Part (d): Anil's summary, settled by (b) and (c)

questions.q: Suppose an Indian lecturer and a British lecturer in the same university post were paid the same. (a) Which of the chapter's examples of unequal treatment would this remove? (b) Name the other two examples in the same list of the chapter that would still remain.
questions.a: (a) The unequal pay for the same posts in the army, civil services or universities. (b) Juries with a British majority that were lenient towards crimes by Europeans against 'natives', and the bar on mixing with Europeans in clubs, trains, specific areas of cities and some public spaces.
s: Part (a): the pay difference would be removed
Part (b): British-majority juries and exclusion from clubs, trains and public spaces remain

questions.q:
A British newspaper of 1880 writes: 'The Queen's promise has been kept. India is governed in her name by the Secretary of State and the Viceroy, and her subjects are cared for exactly like all others.'
(a) What does the chapter say about who governed British India after 1858 and where each was based?
(b) Give one chapter fact about land taxes that contradicts 'cared for exactly like all others'.
(c) Give two chapter facts that contradict 'cared for exactly like all others'.
(d) The editor replies that unequal pay is only a matter of economy. Which statement in the chapter about how Indians were regarded answers him?
questions.a: (a) The Secretary of State for India, based in London, and the Viceroy (also known as Governor General), the Queen's representative based in India. (b) Heavy land taxes resulted in several severe famines and widespread discontent among peasants and tribals. (c) Any two of: lesser pay for Indians in the same posts; British-majority juries lenient to Europeans; exclusion from clubs, trains and public spaces; the Arms Act; the Vernacular Press Act. (d) Indians were regarded as belonging to 'inferior races', the white race asserting that it was destined to dominate the world, so the inequality rested on a belief about race.
s: Part (a): Secretary of State in London; Viceroy in India
Part (b): heavy land taxes, famines and discontent
Part (c): two contradicting facts
Part (d): the belief in 'inferior races'

questions.q: A student writes: 'After 1858 the Viceroy sat in London and the Secretary of State sat in India.' (a) Correct her. (b) Say whose name the territories of British India were now governed in.
questions.a: (a) The Secretary of State for India was based in London, and the Viceroy, also known as Governor General, was the Queen's representative based in India. (b) They were governed in Queen Victoria's name.
s: Part (a): Secretary of State in London; Viceroy in India
Part (b): in the Queen's name

questions.q: Four incidents are reported from an Indian town in the 1880s: (i) an Indian college lecturer is paid less than an English colleague in the same post; (ii) an Indian passenger is told to leave a railway compartment where Europeans sit; (iii) a jury with an English majority acquits a European who beat an Indian porter; (iv) an Indian shopkeeper is fined for keeping a gun while his English neighbour keeps one freely. Name the chapter's example or law each illustrates, and then give the belief the chapter says lay behind all of them.
questions.a: (i) Unequal pay: employees in the army, civil services or universities had lesser pay than British employees in the same posts. (ii) Exclusion from public spaces: in clubs, trains, specific areas of cities and some public spaces Indians were not allowed to mix with Europeans. (iii) British-majority juries, lenient towards crimes committed by Europeans against 'natives'. (iv) The Arms Act of 1878, which prohibited Indians from keeping arms but allowed the British to do so. The belief behind all of them was that Indians belonged to 'inferior races' and that the white race was destined to dominate the world.
s: (i) identified as unequal pay
(ii) identified as exclusion from trains and public spaces
(iii) identified as British-majority juries
(iv) identified as the Arms Act of 1878
The belief in 'inferior races' and a white race destined to dominate

questions.q: True or False: The proclamation's promise that Christianity would not be imposed meant that missionary work received no help from the state after 1858. Give a reason.
questions.a: False. Missionary activity continued with indirect state support, for instance concessions of urban land, and often with open encouragement from British high officials.
s: Verdict: false
Reason: indirect support through urban land concessions and open encouragement from high officials

questions.q:
Match each situation (1-4) with the term it illustrates (a-d).
1. A British officer sits in a prince's court and often interferes in the running of the state.
2. A Tamil newspaper's articles must pass a government censor before they circulate.
3. An Indian villager may not keep a weapon, while his British neighbour may.
4. A prince keeps his throne but is told that Britain is the supreme power.
a. Arms Act    b. Paramountcy    c. Resident or Political Agent    d. Vernacular Press Act

The chapter says the promises of 1858 were 'intended to convey the message that the colonial masters would now prefer to rule in peace than through military force.' Explain how Residents, heavy land taxes and missionary support could each weaken that message for an Indian of the time.
questions.a: A Resident who interfered in a state's government showed the prince that his autonomy was only symbolic. Heavy land taxes caused several severe famines and widespread discontent among peasants and tribals, which is not peaceful rule for them. Missionary activity with state support and open official encouragement went against the assurance of no imposition of Christianity. So each of the three pointed to the same fact, that the assurances were not respected in practice.
s: Residents: autonomy of princely states made symbolic
Heavy land taxes: famines and discontent among peasants and tribals
Missionary support against the assurance, so promises not respected

questions.q: A prince says in 1870: 'The proclamation made my state mine again; the Resident at my court is only a guest.' (a) Which promise of 1858 supports the first half? (b) Which chapter fact makes the second half untrue?
questions.a: (a) The proclamation promised to respect the rights, dignity and honour of the native Princes, so some 560 princes would continue to rule their states, under British supremacy called paramountcy. (b) A Resident or Political Agent was posted in almost all the states and very often interfered in their government and administration, reducing the autonomy to a symbolic one, so he was no mere guest.
s: Part (a): rights, dignity and honour respected; princes keep ruling under paramountcy
Part (b): Residents very often interfered, so autonomy was only symbolic

questions.q: A file reaches a desk in 1865 marked 'from the Governor General'. Where was this officer based, and whom did he represent, according to the chapter?
questions.a: In India, as the Viceroy, representing Queen Victoria
o: In India, as the Viceroy, representing Queen Victoria
In London, as the Secretary of State for India
In a princely state, as the Resident posted at its court
In India, as the head of the East India Company's board

questions.q: The Vernacular Press Act and the Arms Act were both passed in 1878, which was ___ years after the Crown took direct control of India.

Consider these statements about the royal proclamation of 1858.
1. It was issued in Queen Victoria's name.
2. It left the princes free of paramountcy.
3. It assured the natives of the Indian territories that no attempt would be made to impose Christianity.
Which is or are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 only
o: 1 and 3 only
1 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: Compare what the 1858 proclamation promised with what the chapter says happened, covering the princes, the assurance about religion and economic life, and end with what the comparison shows about the 'rule in peace' message.
questions.a: The proclamation promised to respect the rights, dignity and honour of the native Princes, to care for the natives like all other subjects, and not to impose Christianity. For the princes, a Resident or Political Agent was posted in almost all states and interfered, so autonomy became symbolic. On religion, missionary work continued with indirect state support such as urban land concessions and open encouragement from high officials. In economic life, exploitation continued, with heavy land taxes, severe famines and cheap British goods that local industry could not match. The comparison shows that the promises were words meant to convey rule in peace, but none of the assurances were respected in practice.
s: Sets out the three promises of the proclamation
Princes: Residents and Political Agents, symbolic autonomy
Religion: indirect state support and open encouragement for missionaries
Economy: heavy land taxes, famines, cheap British goods
Conclusion: none of the assurances were respected in practice

questions.q: A guide in a museum says: 'The Dictionary of Martyrs lists every Indian who struggled for freedom.' (a) What does the chapter say the Dictionary is and how many it lists? (b) Why does the chapter say the people it names are only a few?
questions.a: (a) It is a five-volume work published by the Indian Council of Historical Research listing some 14,000 heroes and heroines of the freedom struggle. (b) The full story would take many books, and behind the few named stand many more, from every part of India, who are no less important.
s: Part (a): five-volume work of the Indian Council of Historical Research, some 14,000 listed
Part (b): many more stand behind those named, who are no less important

questions.q: A teacher says: 'A person who dies in prison for refusing to give up her beliefs is a martyr.' Which definition from the chapter does she use?
questions.a: A person who is killed or tortured for his or her beliefs
o: A person who is killed or tortured for his or her beliefs
A soldier who dies fighting in a war for his country
A person who is exiled to a distant island for political activity
A leader who is hanged after a trial for sedition

questions.q: What did Indian reformers do with European models while challenging social practices, and which two social practices did they challenge?
questions.a: They took note of European models while challenging social practices. Two practices challenged were child marriage and caste-based discrimination (or the degraded status of widows, or the widespread lack of formal education).
s: Took note of European models
Two practices challenged

questions.q: Anandamath was published in 1882, so the poem Bande Mataram in it had been composed ___ years earlier.
Meera says: 'The Brahmo Samaj and the Arya Samaj were the same movement under two names.' Test the claim against the chapter's table and give a verdict.
questions.a: No. They shared some aims, such as opposing caste discrimination and supporting women's education and widow rights. But the founders, years and places differ: Raja Ram Mohan Roy, 1828, Calcutta, against Swami Dayananda Saraswati, 1875, Bombay. Their ideas also differ: the Brahmo Samaj promoted a monotheistic interpretation of Hinduism and favoured English education, while the Arya Samaj emphasised a return to the Vedas and opposed ritualism.
s: Notes what the two shared
Contrasts founders, years and places
Contrasts their ideas, with verdict no

questions.q: A student reads Vivekananda's advice to 'look back, drink deep of the eternal fountains, and then march forward' and concludes that India should copy its past without change. Which chapter fact shows the conclusion is too narrow?
questions.a: He encouraged science, advising Jamsetji Tata to set up a research institute
o: He encouraged science, advising Jamsetji Tata to set up a research institute
He founded the Brahmo Samaj in Calcutta to oppose ritualism and child marriage
He took part in political action against British rule in Bengal and Punjab
He urged Indians to give up the study of Sanskrit texts and the Vedas

questions.a: He was a sub-magistrate in a district of Bengal, and wrote popular Bengali novels on romance and Indian history
o: He was a sub-magistrate in a district of Bengal, and wrote popular Bengali novels on romance and Indian history
He was a Congress delegate at Bombay, and wrote popular English essays on politics

questions.q: Write a three-sentence label for a postage stamp showing Raja Ram Mohan Roy, using only what the chapter says about his movement.
questions.a: Raja Ram Mohan Roy founded the Brahmo Samaj (earlier Brahmo Sabha) in 1828 at Calcutta. It opposed child marriage and caste discrimination and supported widow rights and girls' education. It promoted a monotheistic interpretation of Hinduism and favoured English education.
s: Founder, name, year and place
Two causes it supported or opposed
Its religious idea and its view of English education

questions.q: A classmate says: 'Bankim changed the spelling of the title to Bande Mataram so that British censors would not understand it.' (a) Give the chapter's actual reason for the 'B'. (b) State what the title means.
questions.a: (a) It is the Bengali version of the Sanskrit 'Vande Mataram', and there is no letter 'va' in Bengali, only 'ba', so the spelling has nothing to do with censors. (b) Literally 'Praise to the Mother' or 'I bow to the Motherland'.
s: Part (a): no 'va' in Bengali; Bengali version of the Sanskrit title
Part (b): Praise to the Mother, or I bow to the Motherland

questions.q: A reform-minded family in the 19th century has two needs. (i) It wants its daughters to go to school and values English education. (ii) A cousin who left Hinduism wants to come back. Using the chapter's table, name the movement that suits each need and give the idea or aim from the table that fits. Then say which of the two movements was led by the leaders of a third movement, naming that third movement.
questions.a: (i) The Brahmo Samaj, founded by Raja Ram Mohan Roy in 1828 at Calcutta, which supported girls' education and favoured English education. (ii) The Shuddhi Movement, whose aim was to reconvert people who had left Hinduism. The Shuddhi Movement was led by leaders of the Arya Samaj, which was founded by Swami Dayananda Saraswati in 1875 at Bombay.
s: (i) Brahmo Samaj named
(i) girls' education and English education given as the fit
(ii) Shuddhi Movement named
(ii) aim of reconversion given
Shuddhi led by Arya Samaj leaders

questions.q: Maya says: 'The table says the Brahmo Samaj was later weakened by internal disagreements, so it achieved nothing.' Test the claim against the table.
questions.a: No. The weakening is recorded, but the same table lists its key ideas and contributions: it opposed child marriage and caste discrimination, supported widow rights and girls' education, promoted a monotheistic interpretation of Hinduism and favoured English education. Being weakened later does not cancel those contributions.
s: Notes the weakening recorded in the table
Lists at least two contributions credited to it
Verdict: no, since weakening later does not cancel its contributions

questions.q: The chapter says Vivekananda rejected blind imitation of the West but encouraged science and had studied Western subjects. Explain what he rejected, what he encouraged, and use his own advice about the past to judge whether the two positions conflict.
questions.a: He rejected blind imitation of the West, that is, copying without looking to India's own roots. He encouraged science, advising Jamsetji Tata to create a research institute that eventually became the Indian Institute of Science, and he had himself studied Western literature, history and philosophy along with ancient Indian texts and classical Indian music. His advice was to look back as far as one can, drink deep of the eternal fountains behind, and then march forward. So the positions do not conflict: he welcomed useful learning but wanted it to be built on India's own foundations rather than on imitation.
s: What he rejected: blind imitation
What he encouraged: science, the Tata research institute
His own study of Western and Indian subjects
His advice to look back and then march forward
Judgement that the positions do not conflict

questions.q: A trust wants to honour a reform movement that supported widow rights and girls' education, opposed child marriage and caste discrimination and favoured English education, but was later weakened by internal disagreements. Which movement in the chapter's table fits?
questions.a: The Brahmo Samaj, founded by Raja Ram Mohan Roy
o: The Brahmo Samaj, founded by Raja Ram Mohan Roy
The Arya Samaj, founded by Swami Dayananda Saraswati
The Shuddhi Movement, led by Arya Samaj leaders
The Ramakrishna Mission, founded by Swami Vivekananda

questions.q: A family wants to follow a movement that stressed a return to the Vedas, rational thinking and self-reliance, opposed ritualism and supported widow remarriage. (a) Which movement of the table is this? (b) Name its founder with the year and place.
questions.a: (a) The Arya Samaj. (b) Swami Dayananda Saraswati, in 1875 at Bombay.
s: Part (a): the Arya Samaj
Part (b): Swami Dayananda Saraswati, 1875, Bombay

questions.q: Born in 1863, Narendranath Datta spoke at a Parliament of the World's Religions in 1893. How old was he and where was the speech?
questions.a: 30 years old, in Chicago

questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

questions.q:
A museum caption reads: 'Swami Vivekananda led a political movement against British rule.' Another caption reads: 'The poem Bande Mataram was written in 1905 for the protests.'
(a) Which chapter statement contradicts the first caption?
(b) What did the Ramakrishna Mission, which he founded, aim to combine?
(c) He was born in 1863 and the chapter says his life lasted 39 years. How old was he at the Chicago speech of 1893, and how many years did he live after it?
(d) Test the second caption: how many years before 1905 was the poem composed, and in which year did the novel containing it appear?
questions.a: (a) He did not involve himself in political action; he urged Indians to discover their inner strength and overcome fear, weakness and self-doubt. (b) Spiritual practice with social service. (c) 1893 minus 1863 is 30 years old; 39 minus 30 is 9 more years. (d) 1905 minus 1875 is 30 years; the novel Anandamath appeared in 1882; the poem was composed long before 1905 and only later became a rallying cry, so the caption is wrong.
s: Part (a): he did not involve himself in political action
Part (b): spiritual practice with social service
Part (c): 30 years old; 9 more years
Part (d): 30 years earlier, in 1875; the novel in 1882; caption wrong

questions.q:
Consider these statements about the poem Bande Mataram.
1. It was composed in 1875, before the novel Anandamath was published.
2. Rabindranath Tagore set it to music and sang it at the 1896 Congress session in Calcutta.
3. The Constituent Assembly adopted it as India's National Anthem in 1950.
Which is or are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 2 only
o: 1 and 2 only
1 only
2 and 3 only

questions.q: A widow in 1880 wants to remarry, and her family also wants their daughter to go to school. Both the Brahmo Samaj and the Arya Samaj appear in the chapter's table. What do the entries say about the two movements on these two matters?
questions.a: Both supported widow rights or remarriage, and education for girls or women
o: Both supported widow rights or remarriage, and education for girls or women
Only the Brahmo Samaj supported them, because the Arya Samaj wanted a return to ritual
Only the Arya Samaj supported them, because the Brahmo Samaj opposed English education
Neither supported them; both worked only on reconversion

questions.q: True or False: Swami Vivekananda wanted Indians to reject Western learning completely and look only to the past. Give a reason.
questions.a: False. He had himself studied Western literature, history and philosophy, and encouraged the cultivation of science, advising Jamsetji Tata to create a research institute. What he rejected was blind imitation of the West.
s: Verdict: false
Reason: studied Western subjects, encouraged science; rejected only blind imitation

questions.q:
Two students explain why Bande Mataram mattered in the protests of 1905. Chitra says: 'It was a slogan invented by the 1905 protesters.' Dinesh says: 'It was an earlier poem that gave spiritual and cultural pride to the cause.'
(a) Who wrote the novel in which the poem appears, and what did the sannyasis in it do with the poem?
(b) What image of the motherland did the sannyasis worship?
(c) At which Congress session in 1896 was it sung, and by whom?
(d) Decide whose reading the chapter supports, and say what the authorities did in 1905 that shows the poem had become a force.
questions.a: (a) Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay; in a key scene they recited the poem. (b) The motherland as the divine mother. (c) The Calcutta session, by Rabindranath Tagore, who had set it to music. (d) Dinesh's: the poem was composed earlier (1875) and invoked spiritual and cultural pride from India's past; in 1905 the authorities banned its public singing in street processions.
s: Part (a): Bankim; the sannyasis recited it in a key scene
Part (b): motherland as the divine mother
Part (c): Calcutta session, Tagore
Part (d): Dinesh's reading; the ban on public singing

questions.q: Vivekananda did not involve himself in political action, yet the chapter lists him among the cultural currents that played a part in the rise of nationalist feelings. Explain how both statements can hold.
questions.a: He urged Indians to discover their inner strength and overcome fear, weakness and self-doubt, which gave people confidence. His 1893 speech in Chicago defended India's civilisation and culture, and his call to go back to ancient roots gave cultural pride. Many freedom fighters drew inspiration from him. So he acted on the mind of the nation rather than on politics directly, and that mattered for nationalism.
s: Notes his message of inner strength and self-confidence
Notes the defence of India's civilisation at Chicago and cultural pride
Links to freedom fighters drawing inspiration, resolving the apparent contradiction

questions.q: A student says only the Arya Samaj opposed caste. (a) What does the table say the Arya Samaj opposed in this respect? (b) Which other movement in the table also opposed a form of caste discrimination?
questions.a: (a) Birth-based caste (and ritualism). (b) The Brahmo Samaj, which opposed child marriage and caste discrimination; the 'other reformers' also challenged caste-based discrimination.
s: Part (a): birth-based caste
Part (b): the Brahmo Samaj (or other reformers) also opposed caste discrimination

questions.q: Zoya says: 'The Congress of 1885 drew delegates from diverse regions and religions.' Test the claim against the chapter.
questions.a: Yes. The chapter says seventy-two delegates from diverse regions and religions attended the first session in Bombay. (It adds that they were mostly drawn from Anglicised upper classes, which limits who was represented, but the claim itself is supported.)
s: Seventy-two delegates at the first session in Bombay
From diverse regions and religions
Verdict: supported

questions.q: A Congress session of the early years passes resolutions asking for greater Indian participation in governance and some reforms. How does the chapter say the colonial government responded?
questions.a: It largely ignored them and granted only minor concessions to the Indian side
o: It largely ignored them and granted only minor concessions to the Indian side
It accepted most of them and gave Indians a meaningful share in governance
It treated each resolution as a demand for independence and answered with force
It welcomed them and set up a joint council of Congress and the Viceroy

questions.q: A student claims: 'Discontent against British rule began only after the Congress of 1885 failed to win concessions.' Test this. The events are: (i) Birsa Munda's Ulgulaan; (ii) the first session of the Congress; (iii) the Kuka attacks on slaughterhouses; (iv) the shooting of the Plague Commissioner of Poona by the Chapekar brothers. Put them in the order in which they happened (by date), find the gap between (iii) and (ii) in years, say which events came after the Congress, and give a verdict.
questions.a: In order of date the events are: (iii) the Kuka attacks of 1872, (ii) the Congress of 1885, (iv) the shooting in Poona in 1897 (the year after the plague of 1896), (i) the Ulgulaan of 1899-1900. The Kuka attacks came 1885 minus 1872 = 13 years before the Congress. The chapter says that the Kukas had challenged British rule by rejecting foreign goods and setting up their own institutions. The events of 1897 and 1899-1900 came after the Congress, when the colonial government had largely ignored its resolutions. The claim is therefore wrong: discontent existed before the Congress and continued after.
s: Correct order of the four events
The 13-year gap
Kuka resistance as discontent before 1885
1897 and 1899-1900 as events after the Congress
Verdict: claim wrong

questions.q:
A student notices an oddity in the chapter's account of the Congress. Allan Octavian Hume had become critical of colonial policies, pointing to them as the cause of poverty in India, and resigned. Yet the Congress he helped to launch in 1885 at Bombay began by expressing full faith in the 'providential character' of British rule and 'unswerving allegiance to the British Crown'.
(a) What did the Congress hope to gain through such loyal resolutions?
(b) What was the government's response?
(c) What did Hume do after resigning in 1882?
(d) Using the response in (b), judge whether the Congress's reasoning was working by the late 1890s, and name one development from 1897 or 1899-1900 that suggests it was not.
questions.a: (a) Greater Indian participation in governance, protection of civil rights and some social and economic reforms, so that growing discontent would subside. (b) The government largely ignored the resolutions, granting only minor concessions and denying meaningful participation. (c) He worked to bring together a group of like-minded Indians. (d) It was not working: the government gave only minor concessions while discontent kept growing, as with the Chapekar brothers' action of 1897 or Birsa Munda's Ulgulaan of 1899-1900.
s: Part (a): participation, civil rights, reforms to calm discontent
Part (b): resolutions ignored, minor concessions
Part (c): worked to bring together like-minded Indians
Part (d): discontent kept growing; one development from 1897 or 1899-1900

questions.q:
A government notice of 1872 says: 'The Kukas are only a religious sect and of no political importance.'
(a) Name two social reforms the Kukas worked for.
(b) Name two ways in which they challenged British rule.
(c) What was the British response to the attacks on slaughterhouses in 1872?
(d) The notice makes two claims, 'religious' and 'no political importance'. Say which is supported by the chapter and which is not.
questions.a: (a) Stopping female infanticide and child marriage, and promoting simplified marriage rituals to end the dowry system. (d) 'Religious' is supported, since the movement stressed spiritual discipline and moral purity; 'no political importance' is not supported, since they challenged British rule and the British responded brutally, and the chapter calls the movement a forerunner of the later mass boycott movements.

questions.q: (a) Which two kinds of targets did the Ulgulaan of 1899-1900 attack, according to the chapter? (b) Which group in the chapter's list of Birsa Munda's opponents does one of these targets point to?

questions.a: The Kukas worked to improve Sikh society by stopping female infanticide and child marriage and ending dowry, which is social reform. Political acts: rejecting foreign goods, own post and courts
Concludes it was socio-religious and political

questions.q: In 1871 a village in Punjab refuses to buy foreign goods, wears simple hand-spun white clothes and runs its own postal system and private courts. Which movement does the chapter link this to, and what does it call it in relation to later movements?

questions.a: Resented plague measures, after which the Chapekar brothers shot the Plague Commissioner and an officer
o: Resented plague measures, after which the Chapekar brothers shot the Plague Commissioner and an officer
Tilak's trial for sedition, after which the three brothers shot the two British officials in Poona
The Surat split in the Congress, after which the brothers left the Congress for good and went to Poona

questions.q: Tilak found the Congress leaders too moderate. Using two details from the chapter, explain how his way of reaching people differed from the early Congress's way.

Tilak's methods: Kesari and the festivals

questions.q: A student says boycott was invented in 1905. True or False: Indians had already used the rejection of foreign goods decades earlier. Give a reason.
questions.a: True. The Kukas rejected foreign goods, wore simple hand-spun white clothes and set up their own postal system and private courts in the 1860s and early 1870s, long before boycott became a national strategy.
s: Verdict: true

questions.q: Compare how four groups responded to discontent in the post-1857 period: the early Congress, the Kukas, the Chapekar brothers and Birsa Munda. State each group's method and then say what the contrast shows about the early Congress.
questions.a: The early Congress passed resolutions calling for dialogue and expressed faith in British rule, hoping reforms would calm discontent. s: Early Congress: resolutions and dialogue with loyal faith

Birsa Munda: Ulgulaan of 1899-1900
Contrast: loyal Congress against harder resistance elsewhere

questions.q: A researcher says: 'The Anushilan Samiti and Abhinav Bharat were the same Bengal society.' Correct this using the chapter.
questions.a: The Anushilan Samiti was set up in Bengal in 1902, with centres in many towns and villages, to give young men intellectual, moral and physical training. Abhinav Bharat was a different society, V.D. Savarkar's, with which Tilak was very closely associated.

questions.a: (a) Bihar, Jharkhand, Odisha and Assam (as well as Bengal). (b) The official motive was a more efficient administration; in reality it was the 'divide and rule' policy, splitting a largely Muslim eastern part from a largely Hindu western part.

questions.q: The chapter says the partition 'had two visible results', one of which 'was not part of the colonial calculations'. Name each result, say which was expected, and explain why it surprised the rulers.
questions.a: The expected result was a sharpened division between the two communities, as most Muslim leaders ended up defending the partition. It surprised the rulers because the partition was intended to divide, yet it led to a mass movement that soon spread beyond Bengal.
s: Expected result: sharpened communal division

Why it surprised: a plan to divide produced a movement that spread

But the unexpected result was not part of the colonial calculations: public meetings, processions and rallies multiplied, joined by students, Vande Mataram was sung and rakhis were tied, and the Swadeshi and Boycott programmes emerged and protests spread beyond Bengal. The judgement is that the partition achieved the division the rulers wanted but also provoked a mass movement they had not planned for, so it only partly achieved their aims.

Unexpected result: wave of protest

Judgement: partly achieved aims, with reasons

Part (c): the sharpened division, the expected result

questions.q: A student says: 'The Khilafat Movement was a foreign issue that only harmed the national movement.' questions.a: It began because the Ottoman Empire was dismembered after World War I and the Caliph's position was shaky; the Ali brothers and Maulana Abul Kalam Azad launched it in 1919 to preserve the Caliph's religious authority. Gandhi saw an opportunity to unite Hindus and Muslims against British rule, and the movement merged with Non-Cooperation, initially increasing Muslim participation and mobilising many Hindus. Some Congress members felt the Caliph's status was of no concern to India, and Jinnah left the Congress at the 1920 session, warning against mixing religion with the independence movement. It died a natural death when Mustafa Kemal abolished the sultanate in 1922 and the Caliphate in 1924. Historians debate its aftermath: it temporarily united Hindus and Muslims but also reinforced the sense of separateness among Indian Muslims. So the claim is only partly supported: it brought gains at first, but had costs.

questions.a: The Motilal Nehru report of 1928, drafted in reaction to the Simon Commission, called for Dominion status, meaning total internal autonomy with Britain still controlling the military and foreign policy and the British king or queen as head of state, like Canada and Australia. With growing popular anger and Britain not ready to grant it, younger leaders such as Jawaharlal Nehru and Subhas Chandra Bose wanted Purna Swaraj, complete independence. The demand was not new: the Nationalist faction had voiced it two decades earlier, Aurobindo in 1908, Hasrat Mohani in 1921 and Savarkar in 1925. The Lahore session resolved in December 1929 that India must sever the British connection and attain Purna Swaraj, as the British government had deprived Indians of freedom and ruined India economically, politically, culturally and spiritually.
